title: Chopin and the Piano
objective: After this level you can describe Chopin's piano music.
summary: Chopin settled in Paris and wrote almost only for piano, including Polish mazurkas (accent on beat two). His rubato bends the melody over a steady left hand.

cards.headline: His body is buried in Paris. His heart rests in a church in Warsaw.
cards.body: Frédéric Chopin left Poland in 1830 and never lived there again. When he died in Paris in 1849, aged 39, he was buried at Père-Lachaise, but his heart was taken home to Warsaw's Church of the Holy Cross. How did a pianist come to mean so much to his country?

cards.headline: A composer who lived at the keyboard
cards.body: Born near Warsaw in 1810, Chopin settled in Paris in 1831. Where Beethoven filled symphonies with orchestra and choir (Level 41), Chopin wrote little but piano music: nocturnes, mazurkas, polonaises. His touch was so delicate that it didn't suit big concert halls, so he preferred intimate settings. Think of the difference between a stadium and a living room.

cards.headline: The mazurka: Poland in three
cards.body: The mazurka is a Polish folk dance for couples, with stamping feet and clicking heels. Its music is in triple time, like Level 4's waltz, but with a strong accent on the second beat: one-TWO-three instead of ONE-two-three. Chopin wrote dozens for piano, and Britannica ties his mazurkas and polonaises to his strong nationalist feeling. Far from home, he kept writing Poland's dances.

cards.headline: Rubato: stolen time
cards.body: Rubato comes from the Italian for 'to rob'. The player stretches some beats and hurries others, for expression. In Chopin's style the left hand keeps a fairly steady tempo while the right hand bends and nudges the melody. Remember Level 4: the beat ticks underneath while the rhythm plays on top. Chopin let the tune lean on the clock without breaking it.

mascot.line: Remember the name: rubato, robbed time. The tune bends; the beat underneath holds.

questions.prompt: Nearly all of Chopin's music was written for which instrument?

options.label: The orchestra and choir
options.rationale: That's Beethoven's Ninth; Chopin wrote little but piano music.

questions.explanation: Chopin wrote little but piano works: nocturnes, mazurkas, polonaises and more.

questions.prompt: When a pianist plays Chopin with rubato in his style, what usually happens?

options.label: Both hands speed up steadily to the end
options.rationale: Rubato stretches and hurries; it isn't a steady speed-up.

options.label: The music stops for a free improvised solo
options.rationale: Rubato bends the written music; it isn't improvisation.

options.label: The left hand stays fairly steady while the right bends
Every note is played exactly on the beat

questions.explanation: Rubato, 'robbed time', stretches some beats and hurries others; in Chopin's style the left hand holds a fairly steady tempo.

questions.prompt: Chopin's mazurkas and Level 4's waltz both move in threes. What sets the mazurka's pulse apart?

options.label: It has two beats per measure, not three
options.rationale: It's triple time, like the waltz.

options.label: It has no regular beat at all
options.rationale: It's a dance: the beat is steady.

options.label: It is always much slower than a waltz
options.rationale: The difference is the accent, not the speed.

options.label: A strong accent falls on the second beat

questions.explanation: Both are triple time, but the mazurka accents the second beat: one-TWO-three.
